paper_metadata.title: Quantum-Assisted AI for Speeding up Large-Scale Data Processing

summary: The paper presents a hybrid QAAI framework using QSVM, QNN, variational quantum circuits, and randomized measurement protocols on IBM Quantum superconducting hardware and simulators. It reports 30-40% faster training overall, 92.5% accuracy versus 85% for traditional SVM in healthcare, 37% training-time reduction in finance, and 93% precision versus 82% for traditional anomaly detection in cybersecurity.

experiments.description: Hybrid quantum-classical QAAI framework for large-scale data processing, evaluated on healthcare classification, finance trend prediction, and cybersecurity anomaly detection using QSVM, QNN, VQCs, randomized measurement protocols, and quantum data encoding on IBM Quantum Experience/PennyLane.

algorithm.variant: QAAI hybrid framework combining QSVM, QNN, and variational quantum circuits
algorithm.ansatz: variational quantum circuits; specific ansatz not reported

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Classical data encoded into quantum states using amplitude encoding for financial data and basis encoding for patient records; quantum kernel estimation used for QSVM; variational gates tuned iteratively in VQCs.

problem_instance.description: Multiple real-world data-processing tasks across healthcare, finance, and cybersecurity.

dataset_specification.description: Healthcare patient diagnostic data; financial stock market trend and real-time trading pattern data; cybersecurity network traffic data. No specific ticker symbols, date range, or split reported.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Normalization, feature scaling, and data balancing; amplitude encoding for financial data; basis encoding for healthcare records; randomized measurement protocols for noise resilience in cybersecurity data.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Performance evaluated across multiple iterations using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score; compared against classical baselines including traditional SVM and traditional machine learning models.

noise_model.noise_type: hardware noise / gate errors / input-data noise

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Normalization, feature scaling, and data balancing.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Metrics computation and comparison against classical baselines.

speedup_claims.baseline_method: conventional AI model / traditional machine learning models
speedup_claims.conditions: high-dimensional datasets; hybrid QAAI framework with VQCs and quantum-enhanced learning
speedup_claims.caveats: Paper reports a range and does not provide raw timing values, dataset sizes, or statistical uncertainty.

speedup_claims.conditions: financial dataset experiment; high-frequency trading / stock market trend prediction

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: IBM Quantum superconducting QPU plus simulators; variational quantum circuits, QSVM, QNN, randomized measurement protocols, and hybrid quantum-classical preprocessing/postprocessing
limiting_factors: No problem size, qubit count, circuit depth, or runtime scaling is reported
Reported gains are empirical percentage improvements only, not asymptotic advantage
Classical baselines remain strong and are explicitly compared against
Data encoding overhead is acknowledged as a limitation
Hardware noise, gate errors, and limited qubit stability are stated as major constraints

notes: IBM Quantum hardware is explicitly named, but no specific device name, qubit count, circuit depth, shot count, optimizer, or ansatz details are reported.
The paper reports empirical speedup claims (30-40% training speed improvement) but does not provide asymptotic complexity orders, so speedup_order is set to none_proven.

The paper reports 30-40% training speed improvement, 92.5% accuracy for QSVM on healthcare data versus 85% for traditional SVM, 37% training-time reduction in finance, and 93% precision for cybersecurity anomaly detection versus 82% for traditional methods.
However, no rigorous quantum advantage demonstration or scaling evidence is provided.
